chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Muhammad ibn Hakim who said:

I said to Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him): May I be your ransom, Allah has given us understanding in the religion and made us self-sufficient through you from the people, so much so that a group of us in a gathering, one man asks his companion about a matter that comes to his mind and receives an answer for it, which is from the mercy of Allah upon us through you; however, it may happen that something is referred to us about which we have received nothing from you or your forefathers, so can we look for the best-match in what we have and the closest to that which has come down to us from you and take it [as the answer]?

So he said: Not at all, not at all, in doing that — by Allah — were destroyed those who were destroyed, O Ibn Hakim. Then he said: May Allah curse Abu Hanifa, he used to say: 'Ali said, but I say.' Muhammad ibn Hakim then reported to Hisham ibn al-Hakam that: By Allah, I did not want anything [in asking this] except that he permit Qiyas (analogical reasoning) for me.

key_terms.أَبُو حَنِيفَةَ: Abu Hanifa, the founder of the Hanafi school of Sunni jurisprudence, often cited in Shia texts as a primary example of using Qiyas.
key_terms.إِبْرَاهِيمُ بْنُ مَيْمُونَ: Ibn Abi Umayr, a prominent narrator known for his reliability and close association with the Imams.
key_terms.الْقِيَاس: Analogical reasoning (Qiyas), a method of deriving legal rulings by comparing a new case to an existing one based on a common cause.
key_terms.فَقَهُنَا: We have gained understanding/jurisprudence, referring to the deep knowledge of the religion possessed by the Shia.

ai.seo_question: What is the Shia view on Qiyas (analogical reasoning) and its relation to Abu Hanifa?
ai.summary: Imam Musa al-Kadhim (AS) rejects the use of independent analogical reasoning (Qiyas) for new issues, warning that it leads to spiritual ruin as it substitutes human opinion for divine guidance. He specifically critiques Abu Hanifa’s method of appending 'I said' to the Prophet’s or Imam’s words, which Shia scholars view as elevating personal reasoning above the established authority of the Ahl al-Bayt. This hadith underscores the Shia principle of relying on transmitted knowledge rather than speculative deduction in jurisprudence.
